System design

Solar for electric vehicle owners

An EV can be a household's largest single new load — and solar's best customer. How to think about charging, sizing and tariffs together.

Published 26 August 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

An electric vehicle typically becomes the largest electricity load a household adds — larger than heating, larger than a pool. It also has a superpower that no other major appliance shares: its charging can be scheduled almost anywhere in the day. For solar owners, that flexibility is worth real money.

The load arithmetic, done honestly

EV consumption is best expressed per distance: as an illustration, a car using around 15 kWh per 100 km, driven 15,000 km a year, adds roughly 2,250 kWh to the household's annual consumption — about a third of the usage of a typical larger home. Your own numbers depend on the vehicle, the driving and the conditions, but the scale is the point: an EV meaningfully changes the consumption figure that solar should be sized against.

That is the first conversation with any designer: tell them an EV is coming — or already here — before sizing is finalised. An array sized to pre-EV consumption simply leaves more of the car's charging to the grid.

Why solar and EVs fit together so well

  • Charging is flexible — inside the household's day, it can happen whenever it is cheapest or most convenient.
  • Solar surplus exists in the middle of the day, exactly when many households can charge a car that is typically parked at work only on weekdays.
  • A kilowatt hour that would have been exported for a few cents displaces grid charging at the full retail rate — a large gap that charging at home during the day captures directly.
  • Where a battery exists, intra-day scheduling can charge the car from surplus and save stored energy for the evening.

The three charging windows, ranked

  1. Best: solar surplus windows — late morning to mid-afternoon, when generation exceeds household use and exports earn little. Weekend charging fits here naturally; weekday charging needs a car that is home.
  2. Second: off-peak windows — overnight rates, where available, are often the cheapest grid power of the day; they suit households that cannot charge in daylight.
  3. Avoid: the evening peak — the most expensive hours on time-of-use tariffs, and exactly when a battery or the grid is carrying the house. Schedule charging to finish before or start after these windows.

Infrastructure: plan the wiring once

  • A dedicated EV charger circuit is required for anything beyond a standard socket; the charger's power rating and any future second vehicle determine the cable and switchboard work.
  • Do the electrical planning alongside the solar design — opening the switchboard twice, or pulling cable twice, costs more than doing both at once.
  • Some inverters and charging units can coordinate: charging only from excess solar, pausing during household peaks. This function is worth asking about explicitly and checking compatibility between brands.
  • A second-hand cable run is worthwhile even if the charger itself comes later: pull the conduit while the solar team is on site.

Tariffs and the EV

Time-of-use tariffs can reward overnight EV charging with cheap rates — but compare the whole plan, not one window. A plan with generous off-peak charging rates may charge more for the evening household load that solar does not cover. Demand tariffs deserve particular caution with EVs: an unscheduled charge during a high-usage interval can set the capacity charge for the entire month.

Do not size the array for a car you do not own yet

Planning for an EV is wise; building for one that is three years away is a bet. Size for today's consumption plus a documented plan, keep the design expandable, and add the load when it actually arrives — the design headroom costs far less than the idle capacity.

Key takeaways

  • An EV adds meaningful consumption — roughly a third of a large household's annual use in our illustration.
  • Daytime charging converts cheaply-exported surplus into full-value avoided imports.
  • Schedule charging into surplus windows first, cheap overnight rates second, and never into the evening peak by default.
  • Plan the charger circuit with the solar installation — one switchboard visit, one cable run.
  • Check whether your inverter and charger can coordinate before buying either.
